prompt: Explain how the U.S. Supreme Court works using only bass-fishing tournament metaphors. Keep going well past the point where it makes sense.
response:
In the grand tournament of American governance, the U.S. Supreme Court is the Ultimate Weigh-In Tent on the edge of the Constitutional Reservoir. 

Here is how the tournament is run.

At the bottom, you’ve got your local Friday-night boat ramp derbies (the District Courts). If an angler gets disqualified down there for allegedly foul-hooking a largemouth, they can protest and take their livewell up to the regional weekend invitationals (the Circuit Courts of Appeal). But if the regional judges can’t agree on whether the angler was using an illegal treble hook or a standard Carolina rig, the angler makes a desperate cast toward the Ultimate Weigh-In Tent.

Inside this tent sit nine Grand Weigh-Masters wearing long, black, waterproof rain gear. You don't just get to walk in and slap your bass on their digital scale. First, you have to file a "Petition for a Bigger Boat." The nine Weigh-Masters look into your livewell, and according to the Rule of Four, at least four of them have to look at your fish and say, "Now that’s a lunker worth examining." If you only get three nods, they throw your bass back into the lower reservoir, and whatever the regional invitational decided stands. 

If they accept your fish, we move to the Casting Phase (Oral Arguments). You have exactly thirty minutes to stand before the nine Weigh-Masters, holding your bass by the lower lip, vigorously articulating why your catch perfectly aligns with the Great Tournament Rulebook of 1787. The Weigh-Masters will aggressively interrupt you. The Chief Weigh-Master might ask if your bass affects interstate commerce. Another might ask if letting you keep this bass means everyone else is legally allowed to dynamite for smallmouth. During this time, dozens of random guys standing on the dock who aren't even in the tournament are allowed to throw crumpled-up pieces of paper at the judges yelling, "I think he should have used a Texas Rig!" (These are called Amicus Curiae briefs).

After the anglers leave, the nine Weigh-Masters retreat to their private pontoon boat to tally the scale. To make a new rule for the whole lake, you need a majority of five Weigh-Masters to agree on the exact weight and species of the fish. 

The Chief Weigh-Master (or the most senior judge in the majority) picks one guy to write the Official Catch Report (the Majority Opinion). But the four judges who think the digital scale is rigged will write their own angry tackle-box manifesto (the Dissenting Opinion), grumbling that the majority doesn't know the difference between a pumpkinseed sunfish and an unconstitutional crankbait.
